newsitem.title: SPAIN: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish CPI falls to 2.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish CPI falls to 2.9 pct.

text.p: Following is a selection of reactions to Spanish data showing consumer inflation was 0.3 percent in January month-on-month, bringing the year-on-year rate down to 2.9 percent from 3.2 percent in December.
Core inflation was 0.2 percent month-on-month, or 2.8 percent year-on-year.
CARMEN HERNANSANZ, ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH.

"It's a very good figure. The general index is as we forecast but the core rate is even lower. The fall in some regulated prices must have helped this figure. After this data I think the Bank of Spain has room to cut rates by 25 basis points (from 6.00 percent) tomorrow. The Bank of Spain wanted inflation below three percent in 1997 and it's got it in January"
ANTONI ESPASA, DIRECTOR OF BOLETIN IPC - CARLOS III AND PRICE WATERHOUSE

"This data is better-than-expected, especially in core CPI but I think it is due mainly to the decline in processed food (down 0.3 percent in the month and up 1.8 percent in the year). That means olive oil declines had a greater-than-expected effect but I do not think this will change the whole picture for the year.
Pressure could came from markets, which were expecting worse data, but otherwise the Bank of Spain will wait and will not cut its money market rate tomorrow.
I think the Bank of Spain was expecting data like that. They have in mind that Spanish inflation perspectives for 1998 are not as positive as this year's and so they will hold."
BELEN MATEOS, ECONOMIST OF ANALISTA FINANCIEROS INTERNACIONALES (AFI)

"The data was very good. Processed foods and energy prices have behaved particularly well. I would only put a note of caution in service prices, as the Bank of Spain has already warned. The overall valuation is positive, and in fact, the Bank of Spain has a good opportunity to lower rates tomorrow. It has enough scope, although the peseta could be a point of caution although it is not worrying."
MARK GEDDES, TREASURY ECONOMIST AT 4CAST LTD RESEARCH

"(The CPI is) pretty good really, already within range for the Bank of Spain's 1997 target (2.5 percent). The trend is very very favourable, the question is whether we're going to see another rate cut. The figures are better than expected so that would leave room for optimism, but I'd say look at mark/peseta. It's managed to fight off some of the recent speculative pressure, and although I'd be on the cautious side, if we see a recovery to under 84.50 (to the mark) we might see a rate cut tomorrow."
COLIN WARREN, ECONOMIST AT TOKAI BANK IN LONDON

"The January CPI is good but if you look at the breakdown, it is not in favour of the Bank of Spain cutting rates tomorrow. They will prefer to wait for the February data and perhaps, for the labour deals."
MARIA VICTORIA NUNEZ, JUNIOR ECONOMIST AT SOCIETE GENERALE IN MADRID

"The valuation of the data is very positive. At the end, the energy prices have had a very positive evolution, and that has been evident in the year-on-year rate. There is no doubt that this number increases the possibilities that tomorrow, there will be a decline in the official price of money. In my opinion, the Bank of Spain could cut rates by 25 basis points tomorrow because of this figure."
JUAN ANTONIO MIELGO, BANK OF AMERICA IN MADRID - RFTV
"CPI will raise expectations of an easing. We continue to forecast the Bank of Spain will cut rates by 50 basis points tomorrow."
ANDREA DELITALIA, FIXED-INCOME STRATEGIST - RFTV
"This shouldn't mean the central bank will lower rates tomorrow. They will still wait for confirmation in February." CESAR MOLINAS, FG INVERSIONES - RFTV
"There is no hurry in shaving official rates. In spite of this, we see a 50/50 chance of a 25 basis point cut tomorrow.
"I think the (inflation) target of ending the year around 2.5 percent has a fair chance.
"Hitting Maastricht has a pretty large probability of 70 percent."
VALENTIN FERNANDEZ, CHIEF ECONOMIST OF CREDIT LYONNAIS IN MADRID

"It is a good number, for the overall inflation as well as for the underlying. Processed food contributed the most to this figure. One-tenth better than what was being forecast means that the market is divided 50 percent between those that believe the Bank of Spain is going to cut and 50 percent that believe it will not due, principally, to the recent episodes that have affected the peseta. I believe that there is more than a 50-percent chance that the Bank of Spain doesn't do anything tomorrow although the data allows one to think there is scope. The number today confirms that this year, we will have European inflation."
--Madrid Newsroom +34 1 585 2167
